sec: Alport: electron microscopy, transplant & thin GBM disease · p784

items.q: Match each Alport syndrome finding with the investigation that shows it — 1) Splitting and lamellation of the lamina densa  2) No immune deposits  3) Normal glomerular architecture on routine staining … A) Immunofluorescence  B) Light microscopy  C) Electron microscopy
items.exp: In Alport syndrome light microscopy and immunofluorescence are normal, the diagnosis resting on electron microscopy, which shows splitting and lamellation of the lamina densa with alternating thick and thin foci and a basket-weave appearance. (Book p784)

items.q: The electron-microscopy appearance described in Alport syndrome is:
opts: Splitting and lamellation of the lamina densa with a basket-weave appearance
Subepithelial camel-hump deposits with a starry sky pattern on IF
Intramembranous dense-body deposits with tram-track capillary duplication
Uniformly thin glomerular basement membrane without any lamellation
items.exp: EM in Alport syndrome: splitting + lamellation of the lamina densa, alternating thick and thin foci, giving a basket-weave appearance. (Book p784)

items.q: Light microscopy and immunofluorescence are typically normal in Alport syndrome, the diagnosis resting on electron microscopy.
opts: False — LM shows crescents in all cases
False — IF shows linear IgG in all cases
True, but only in the autosomal dominant form
items.exp: Investigation in Alport syndrome: LM and IF are normal; EM shows splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa with a basket-weave pattern. (Book p784)

items.q: The treatment given for Alport syndrome in the book is:
items.exp: Rx in Alport syndrome: transplant — with the post-transplant complication of Goodpasture syndrome (antibody against α3). (Book p784)

items.q: What percentage of Alport patients develop Goodpasture syndrome as a complication after transplantation?
items.exp: Complication post-transplant in Alport syndrome: 5% develop Goodpasture syndrome, from antibodies against α3 (collagen). (Book p784)

items.q: A man with Alport syndrome received a kidney transplant; 8 months later anti-GBM antibody is detected. Which explanation fits the book?
opts: Antibody against α3 collagen of the graft — post-transplant Goodpasture syndrome in 5%
Recurrence of Alport syndrome in the graft in 50%
Recurrent PSGN from a streptococcal throat infection
items.exp: Alport syndrome post-transplant: 5% develop Goodpasture syndrome due to antibody against α3, because the native α3 had never been 'seen' by the immune system. (Book p784)

items.q: Thin GBM disease is inherited as and caused by:
items.exp: Thin GBM disease: AD, COL4A4/A3 mutation. (Book p784)

items.q: Match thin GBM disease features with their descriptions — 1) Clinical features  2) Light microscopy and IF  3) Electron microscopy … A) Uniformly thin (<200–300 nm)  B) Normal  C) Microscopic haematuria (<5 years) with good prognosis
items.exp: Thin GBM disease: microscopic haematuria (<5 years) with good prognosis; LM and IF normal; EM shows a uniformly thin GBM (<200–300 nm). (Book p784)

items.q: On electron microscopy, the glomerular basement membrane in thin GBM disease measures:
items.exp: EM in thin GBM disease: uniformly thin GBM, <200–300 nm. (Book p784)

items.q: Thin GBM disease usually has a good prognosis, presenting with microscopic haematuria below 5 years of age.
opts: False — it progresses to ESRD by 30 years
False — it presents with nephrotic syndrome
items.exp: Thin GBM disease clinical features: microscopic haematuria (<5 years) and good prognosis; LM/IF are normal with EM showing a uniformly thin GBM. (Book p784)

items.q: All but one of the following are seen in thin GBM disease. Which is the odd one out?
opts: Basket-weave splitting of the lamina densa
items.exp: Basket-weave splitting/lamellation of the lamina densa belongs to Alport syndrome; thin GBM disease simply shows a uniformly thin GBM on EM. (Book p784)
